stories.headline: Israel votes in its first election since the October 7 attack, with Netanyahu facing a pivotal test

sources.body: Israelis head to the polls on Tuesday for the first time since Hamas's October 7, 2023 attack, in a closely contested election seen as a referendum on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The vote follows three years of regional wars, with Netanyahu running neck and neck with centrist rival Gadi Eisenkot.
sources.headline: Israel votes in first election since October 7 attack as Netanyahu faces crucial test

sources.body:
Netanyahu seeks to extend rule at helm of far right alliance facing off against predominantly right-wing bloc.

Israel is heading to the polls on Tuesday in a closely contested election that is being described as one of the most important in its history.

The vote is the first since the Hamas-led attack of October 7, 2023 and the subsequent genocidal war against Palestinians in Gaza, as well as a wider conflict that has seen Israel carry out attacks on Iran, Lebanon, Yemen, Syria and Qatar.

Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, is seeking to extend his tenure after leading the country’s most right-wing governing coalition which brought together far-right ultranationalists and ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties.

Wanted by the International Criminal Court on charges of war crimes in Gaza and faced with a long-running corruption trial, he is fighting for his political survival against a self-styled Zionist opposition bloc that has fundamentally embraced a right-wing approach to Israel’s challenges. Questions over accountability for alleged security failures , disputes over ultra-Orthodox military service and efforts to exclude Arab-led parties dominated the campaign.

This has further dampened already low expectations that the vote would offer any meaningful improvement to the lives of Palestinians, as deadly attacks continue almost daily in Gaza despite a yearlong “ceasefire”, while settler pogroms and Israeli army raids have intensified in the occupied West Bank.

“The entire Israeli political system operates within the racist framework of Jewish supremacy,” Yehouda Shenhav-Shahrabani, a noted Israeli sociologist, told Al Jazeera.

“None of the leaders who present themselves as an alternative to Netanyahu can genuinely be described as left-wing. The horrifying reality we are witnessing is not simply the product of Netanyahu or the far right. It is rooted in Zionist political thought itself, which is structured around the principle of Jewish supremacy. There is no way around this fundamental fact,” he said.

Israel’s shift to the right did not begin with the establishment of Netanyahu’s most recent government in 2022, or what polls show to have been the rightward lurch that took place across Israel following the Hamas-led attack of 2023. Rather, the collapse of the peace process with the Palestinians and repeated security crises over the past few decades have combined to systematically erode the political centre and left, giving rise to landmark legislative milestones such as the 2018 Nation-State Law , which formally enshrined Jewish supremacy and the continued and violent expansion of illegal Israeli settlements into occupied Palestinian territory with little or no government restraint.

However, if the drift to the right was there beforehand, most analysts agree that its speed has accelerated to unprecedented heights under the latest Netanyahu government, which faced accusations of seeking to reshape the country in its own image

They point to attempts to strip the Supreme Court of its power to review government actions and the flouting of its rulings on conscripting the ultra-Orthodox minority whose political support helped sustain the governing coalition, as well as the presence of figures such as far-right provocateur and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and religious Zionist Bezalel Smotrich , Israel’s finance minister.
sources.headline: Israel heads to the polls as shift to the right dominates critical election

sources.body:
In the next week, two sets of elections will be held on two continents, the outcomes of which could have profound consequences for the world.

By a fluke of electoral timetabling, millions of voters around 6,000 miles apart will unite in exercising their democratic rights within days of each other.

Voters in Israel go to the polls on Tuesday to elect a new parliament; a week later, voters in the United States will elect a new Congress.

A former speaker of that Congress, Tip O'Neill, may have once said that "all politics is local". But the consequences of these elections will undoubtedly be global.

For these elections are not just proximate, they are intertwined.

The future governance of Israel will have a lasting impact on the Middle East and wars raging across the region.

And any change in the electoral map of America could shape not just those wars but also the future of the global economy.

Between the two there is a physical connection: the lobby group Republicans Overseas Israel estimates about half a million Israelis with American passports can vote in both polls.

Marc Zell, the group's chairman, said these electors could influence tight races in the US, such as the Michigan senatorial contest, in which he estimated 10,000 absentee ballots would be cast from Israel. "They can really make a difference," he told the BBC.

But the policy connection is perhaps deeper - and most acute regarding the US-Israeli war on Iran. The massive aerial attack, which began in February, destroyed many military targets and killed much of Iran's leadership. But it failed to overthrow the regime which hit back hard across the Gulf and seized control of the Strait of Hormuz and the energy that flowed through it.

The sheer fact of the elections has already shaped decision-making.

Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has used the campaign to talk up the possibility of launching a fresh attack on Iran.

He has made new claims – without providing evidence – about Iran's nuclear threat, insisting again the Islamic regime must be overthrown.

His aim: to shore up his reputation as a security leader, which took such a battering after the deadly 7 October Hamas-led attacks on Israel.

US President Donald Trump has added to the speculation of renewed attacks on Iran by endorsing Netanyahu's re-election campaign, saying both men should "soon finish the job" in Iran.

Yet for all the sabre-rattling, there have also been contradictory reports that Trump intervened to restrain Netanyahu from attacking Iran before polling day, fearing a fresh spike in energy prices would remind US voters of his unpopular war.

So might an attack on Iran, then, be delayed until after the elections? Israel's media is full of speculation Netanyahu could try to engineer his survival by attacking Iran as caretaker prime minister after the election.

He would argue, so the theory goes, for a government of national unity – involving him – rather than a coalition between opposition parties. Netanyahu has long been seen as a great survivor of Israeli politics. If he were to lose power, he would face an official inquiry into his actions before the October 7 attacks and renewed legal proceedings involving allegations of corruption.
sources.headline: Israel and the US are both going to the polls - the consequences will be global

stories.headline: Regional powers hold talks with Iran to avert renewed Middle East conflict

sources.body: Senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan held talks in Iran on Monday aimed at preventing renewed fighting in the Middle East, with Tehran describing discussions as “very good”. The diplomatic push, attended by Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, followed warnings from Washington, Tehran and Israel of renewed hostilities.
sources.headline: Mecca pact nations hold talks with Iran to prevent renewed Middle East war

sources.body:
Top officials from four countries to continue talks for peace and security as Saudi forces down more Houthi missiles and drones.

Iran and Mecca defence pact countries agree to further talks amid US war threats

Saudi Arabia, Iran, Turkiye and Pakistan have agreed to continue talks for regional “peace and security” as the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen said it had intercepted another barrage of missiles and drones fired by the Houthis at the kingdom.

The talks in Tehran on Monday were the first high-level ‌‌contact between Iran and the three nations – which signed the Mecca mutual defence pact in August – since a war that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran also spread to Saudi Arabia and Yemen.

In a joint statement issued late on Monday, the four countries “agreed to continue the dialogue to strengthen cooperation amongst the four regional countries, including for peace and security in the region,” according to Iranian state media.

Hours later, early on Tuesday, Colonel Turki al-Maliki, a spokesman for the coalition, said that three ballistic missiles fired by the Houthis and aimed at Saudi Arabia’s Eastern Province had been intercepted, causing no casualties. Four drones headed towards the kingdom’s south were also shot down, he said.

The coalition said it had downed three more drones over Riyadh and southern Saudi Arabia on Monday evening.

There was no immediate comment from the Houthis.

Saudi Arabia said the visit to Tehran was meant to open negotiating channels to “prevent the return of military escalation”. The kingdom sent its defence minister, Prince Khalid bin Salman, a younger brother of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. Pakistan sent its army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, and Turkey sent its intelligence chief, Ibrahim Kalin.

Iranian state media published pictures of Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, attending the meetings.

A senior Pakistani security official told the Reuters news agency that the talks focused on building a regional non-aggression network. The official said the agenda also covered negotiations between the US and Iran, the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, the Strait of Hormuz and the US blockade of Iranian ports.

Another Pakistani official told Reuters that Field Marshal Munir, with US President Donald Trump’s blessing to pursue diplomacy, had presented Iran with a proposal that would offer something to both Washington and Tehran. The agency said the official did not give details.

The states in the Mecca pact, along with Qatar, could act as guarantors if the proposal was accepted, the official said.

Rezaei, the Iranian security chief, meanwhile said the visit showed that “American threats have little impact on countries around the world”. He also spoke of a “new and positive atmosphere” in the region.

Esmaeil Baghaei, a spokesman for Iran’s Foreign Ministry, had said earlier that the meeting, proposed when Field Marshal Munir visited Tehran last week, could be a first step towards regional security arrangements.
sources.headline: Iran, Saudi, Turkiye and Pakistan agree to more talks amid Houthi attacks

stories.headline: Jordan strikes targets in Syria in retaliation for a church attack

sources.body:
Jordanian air force says it carried out strikes against ‘terrorist groups’ tied to killing of nine in Karak

Jordan has carried out airstrikes against armed groups in Syria in retaliation for Friday’s attack on a Greek Orthodox church in the southern Jordanian city of Karak that killed nine people, the Jordanian air force has said in a statement.

It said the operation “resulted in the killing and wounding of many members of these terrorist groups and the destruction of a number of their vehicles”. It did not specify who the groups were or the precise location of the strikes.

Syrian state media reported that civilians had been killed in the strikes. The director of health in the southern province of Daraa, where the strikes took place, told the Syrian national news agency, Sana, that at least five civilians had been killed, including women and children and a 65-year-old man.

Jordan’s armed forces said the operation was conducted in coordination with Damascus, but Syria’s government gave a contradictory account, saying it had launched an investigation into the ⁠Jordanian attacks, and stressed in a statement the importance of field and security coordination in border areas.

In the aftermath of the strikes, Syria said it had closed the ⁠Nassib border crossing with Jordan, suspending ⁠traffic in both directions. Nassib is Jordan’s only passenger and commercial border crossing with Syria.

Earlier on Monday, Jordanian authorities arrested three men for last week’s attack, which also wounded more than two dozen people. The arrests followed a dawn shootout, and all three men were wounded, officials said.

The attack struck the Greek Orthodox church during a funeral in Karak, about 55 miles (90km) south of the capital, Amman, on Friday. Karak is home to a minority Christian population.

The attack shocked the nation, and Jordan declared three days of mourning for the victims. No group immediately claimed responsibility for the attack; the attackers’ motive remained unknown.

Later on Monday, Jordan’s Public Security Directorate identified the three arrested men as brothers Hazzah Zaidan Mohammad and Mishal Zaidan Mohammad, and their brother-in-law Ahmad Sami Hussein. All three are Jordanian; they were taken into custody in Karak, south of Amman.

The agency’s chief described the gunmen as “takfiri”, a term used for Sunni militants, but said they were not tied to any organised group.

“They only represent themselves,” Maj Gen Obaidallah Abd Rabbo Al-Maayta told a news conference. He also said a large cache of munitions was found in the abandoned house where Jordanian forces apprehended the men.

Jordan’s interior minister, Mazen al-Faraya, said the attack by the three men was the result of “a terroristic, extremist way of thinking”.

“If this way of thinking is not resolved, we will see incidents like this again,” he told reporters.

Jordan’s King Abdullah II had ordered authorities to respond with “an iron fist” against what he called the outlaws of Islam and anyone attempting to undermine the unity of the Jordanian people.
sources.headline: Jordan attacks militants in Syria in retaliation for last week’s church attack

sources.body:
Syria closes border crossings with Jordan after air strikes kill seven people in Deraa and Suweyda, including children.

Jordan has carried out air strikes in Syria in “retaliation” for last week’s deadly church attack , with Syrian authorities saying the raids killed at least seven people, including three children and a woman.

The attacks on Monday prompted Syria to close its main crossing with Jordan.

Jordan’s Armed Forces said in a statement that it targeted “hideouts” of armed groups in southeastern Syria in response to the gun attack at a church in its Karak governorate on Friday. At least nine people were killed and dozens more wounded in the shootings.

The Jordanian military said the strikes on Syria were launched “in coordination with the Syrian government”.

It said the raids “resulted in the killing and wounding of many members of these terrorist groups and the destruction of a number of their vehicles”.

Syria, however, denied any coordination with Jordan.

In a statement, the Syrian government said “the military operation was conducted without prior coordination or notification” and said it has launched an investigation.

Syria’s Civil Defence service said at least four sites in rural Deraa and Suweyda provinces were hit on Monday evening, and that its crews had recovered the bodies of seven people: three men, a woman and three children.

Five of the dead – a man, a woman and three children – were members of one family killed in a strike on a tent in the village of Al-Tai in Deraa Province, the service said. Three other family members, including a child, were wounded.

A second strike hit Al Shayyah, also in Deraa, killing an 80-year-old man. A third hit a residential building in Muzayrib, in the Ain al-Basal area of Deraa, causing no casualties.

A fourth struck a residential building in the town of Shahba in Suweyda province, killing a 60-year-old man.

After the strikes, Syria’s border authority closed the Nassib crossing, suspending traffic in both directions. Nassib is the only crossing for passengers and commercial goods between Jordan and Syria.

A Syrian Foreign Ministry official called the strikes a “treacherous attack” and told Al Jazeera that the ministry would try to manage the fallout in a way that preserved Syrian sovereignty.

Earlier on Monday, Jordanian security forces arrested two brothers and their brother-in-law on suspicion of involvement in the church attack. The arrests took place in the village of Al-Jadeeda, after a shootout with authorities.

A Jordanian government source told Al Jazeera that the suspects sustained serious injuries during the confrontation, which lasted for about three hours.

The arrests and air strikes in Syria come after Jordan’s King Abdullah II pledged a stern response to the church attack. During the incident, three gunmen opened fire on mourners at a funeral in a Greek Orthodox church in Karak, about 90km south of the capital, Amman.

The king said those responsible would face the “harshest penalties” and ordered a review of the country’s security procedures.
sources.headline: Jordan strikes Syria after church attack, killing at least seven people

stories.headline: UN panel accuses Israel of crimes against humanity in the West Bank and genocide in Gaza

sources.body:
Report finds extermination, torture and rape in the West Bank and says genocide in Gaza is continuing despite a ceasefire.

A United Nations commission of inquiry has accused Israel of committing crimes against humanity in the occupied West Bank, including extermination, torture and rape, while also continuing “to commit genocide in Gaza” despite a ceasefire brokered by the United States.

The report, published on Monday by the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, examined killings and physical and mental harm inflicted by state actors from October 7, 2023, through September of this year.

It was released the day before Israel’s general election .

The commission found that the situation in the West Bank, which Israel has occupied since 1967, had “deteriorated gravely” since the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel on October 7, 2023.

It said Israeli military operations , reinforced by sustained violence by settlers, amounted to a “widespread and systematic attack” on civilians, and that Israeli authorities “intended to collectively punish” residents of the occupied West Bank for the Hamas-led attack on Israel.

“The Israeli authorities and forces have committed the crimes against humanity of extermination, torture, rape and other forms of sexual violence in the West Bank, as well as persecution based on intersecting discriminatory grounds, with nationality, race and ethnicity at its core,” the report said.

The commission also found a sharp rise in deaths from air strikes in the territory.

Six Palestinians were killed in air attacks in the occupied West Bank from 2008 to October 6, 2023, it said, compared with 254 from October 7, 2023, to September 30, 2026.

“The intentional killing and injuring of Palestinian civilians and destruction of homes in the West Bank combined with Israel’s persistent denial of responsibility form part of a broader strategy to exterminate and displace Palestinians and impose conditions of life that are unlivable,” said Srinivasan Muralidhar, the commission’s chair.

“Meanwhile, Israel’s expansion of territorial control in Gaza continues to result in the killing and harming of Palestinian civilians who approach or cross” the so-called Yellow Line that demarcates Israeli-controlled areas in the enclave, he said.

Israel’s mission in Geneva called the report part of the commission’s “misinformation campaign to demonize the State of Israel and portray its very existence as criminal”.

“The international community must reject these distortions, repudiate the commission’s findings and demand its immediate dissolution,” the mission said in a statement.

The commission, which does not speak for the UN as a whole, first concluded in September 2025 that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza during the war that followed the October 7 attacks. Israel has flatly rejected the UN commission’s finding.

In its new report, the commission said Israeli forces had continued to commit “genocidal acts” against Palestinians in Gaza despite the ceasefire brokered by the US last October, with attacks intended to “destroy the Palestinian people, in whole or in part”.
sources.headline: UN panel accuses Israel of ‘extermination’ in West Bank, genocide in Gaza

sources.body: The United Nations on Monday raised "ethnic cleansing" concerns following Israel's operation to displace by force more than 3,000 Palestinians from their homes in Hebron in the West Bank after two Palestinian gunmen killed two Israeli soldiers at a checkpoint near the city on Friday. UN rights chief Volker Turk said in a statement that the "aggressive operation" must end, and that "collective punishment is a grave violation of international law".
sources.headline: UN cites 'ethnic cleansing' concerns around Israel's Palestinian displacement operation in Hebron

stories.headline: Chinese markets lose trillions as the US-China AI race weighs on investors

sources.body:
Lack of profits and the threat posed by western countries are raising concern about the sustainability of Beijing’s AI boom

Trillions of dollars have been wiped from China’s stock markets in recent months amid increasing anxiety about the future of artificial intelligence, as Beijing races against the United States for dominance in the sector.

The STAR 50 Index, which tracks technology and innovation companies on the Shanghai stock exchange, has plunged 40% since June. Other indexes of major companies dropped by about 20% over the same time period.

The precipitous drop has wiped out $2.4tn from the Chinese stock market since May, according to Bloomberg.

AI stocks account for over 40% of the stock market value in China and Hong Kong, according to Goldman Sachs, meaning that any dent in value will send shockwaves across the whole domestic market.

The fall suggests that despite the government’s best efforts to boost China’s technology industries, particularly those which harness the power of AI, the domestic economy does not have the power to sustain a booming market.

The Chinese government has invested heavily into AI, including a 60bn yuan state-backed AI investment fund which started pumping money into domestic developers this month. But Chinese consumers have proved stubbornly reluctant to part with their cash in many parts of the economy – including technology – meaning that many tech companies struggle to turn a profit.

The lack of profits is one of several reasons for the sell-off. Another is the threat of western countries, especially the US, extending bans on Chinese technology.

“This year, the profit margin is not as good as expected. And the US is raising rates. And China’s domestic demand is so weak,” said Dan Wang, the China director for the Eurasia Group. She said that there was a “general anxiety” among technology companies about whether or not the state-backed model would work in the face of weak consumer demand.

The US has banned humanoid robots from China , citing national security risks, and is thought to be considering a ban on Chinese components in data centres. China is heavily reliant on exports and restrictions in the US hurt its domestic companies, which struggle to sell enough products at home.

As China races with the US to pull ahead in AI, Beijing has doubled down on robotics – also known as embodied AI – as the key to rolling out the technology across society. Robotics is also seen as the answer to China’s demographic problems, such as the ageing population and the shrinking workforce.

But the demand for robotics is being driven by government agencies and research institutions, rather than everyday consumers, for whom the products are still too expensive and not yet practical for home use. Humanoid robotics and robotic dogs have been popular in the entertainment industry but are yet to be useful in home settings.

Shares in Unitree, China’s leading robot-maker, have halved since they started trading in August.

“It doesn’t look like embodied intelligence could turn into profits in the in the mass market,” said Wang. Thin profit margins, rising rates in the US, and weak domestic demand were all contributing to a “general anxiety” among technology companies, she said.
sources.headline: Chinese markets lose trillions as race for AI supremacy with US takes its toll

stories.headline: Anthropic’s IPO filing reveals soaring revenue, deep losses and warnings of catastrophic AI risk

sources.body:
Anthropic has warned artificial intelligence (AI) could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity" as it unveiled details of its planned blockbuster stock market listing in the US.

The firm's valuation is expected to exceed that of SpaceX, which was the biggest-ever listing at an initial valuation of about $1.8 trillion in the summer.

Anthropic has not yet disclosed the number of shares to be released, their price range, or a date for the listing.

The Claude chatbot developer reported $16.3bn (£12.2bn) of revenue in the first half of the year, with losses of more than $80.7bn.

Anthropic, which said it will list on the Nasdaq under the symbol ANT, will be the first fully AI-focused company to go public, making it a test case for the future of the technology.

In a filing ahead of its listing, Anthropic said concerns had been raised by policymakers, regulators and researchers as well as by people within its organisation that AI systems posed a significant risk to humanity.

It said advanced AI systems "could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponised, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy".

Anthropic was founded five years ago by chief executive Dario Amodei, his sister Daniela Amodei and five others, and announced its intention to go public in June.

Its main rival, OpenAI, quickly followed suit. That listing is now expected to occur early next year, according to a person familiar with OpenAI's plans.

Those announcements were followed by a wave of cyber-security and other technological breaches involving their AI agents - bots designed to operate somewhat autonomously.

Current and former staff of both companies also warned AI technology was being developed without the ability to protect humanity from possible future harms enacted by AI tools.

As Anthropic revealed its stock debut plans on Monday, the owners of the rights to Elvis Presley's music sued the AI firm accusing it of using hundreds of the rock-and-roll star's songs to train its chatbot Claude.

In Anthropic's new documents, it reiterated promises it has made in the past to develop AI in a way that is beneficial to people, while at the same time warning investors of its dangers.

Anthropic detailed losses in its financial filings that exceeded its revenue for the first half of the year, but said it would often make forward investments "that may seem irresponsibly large at first glance".

"In general, we will aim to be bold but sane, and to win trust with a track record of successful bets," the tech giant said.

Its success depends largely on its ability to develop the most advanced AI models, Anthropic said, adding, "any failure to do so could adversely affect our business".

Across about 90 pages detailing possible risk factors, Anthropic set out the potential threats to its ability to safely and competitively develop AI.
sources.headline: Anthropic warns of 'catastrophic risk' to humankind ahead of blockbuster share listing

sources.body: AI giant Anthropic has publicly filed for an initial public offering (IPO) with US market regulators. The document offered a glimpse into the company's finances but also contained nearly 100 pages related to risks around investing in the company. The filing revealed that in the first half of 2026, its revenue soared to $16.3 billion while net loss widened to over $80 billion. Plus, London's iconic Oxford Street, one of Europe's busiest shopping areas, has been partially pedestrianised.
sources.headline: Anthropic's IPO filing shows soaring sales and steep losses

stories.headline: French student leaders call for continued protests despite government concessions

sources.body: The French government met student representatives on Monday (October 26) following weeks of unrest. Students who had been demanding a meeting for weeks hail progress. Nonetheless they are now calling for fresh demonstrations next Saturday (October 31) to press for further measures. Details by FRANCE 24’s French Politics Editor Marc Perelman.
sources.headline: French student union leaders call for 'continued mobilisation' after meeting PM

sources.body:
Se espera que este lunes sea una fecha clave para el devenir de las protestas en Francia. El primer ministro, Sébastien Lecornu, ha recibido a los representantes de los estudiantes de secundaria, que desde mediados de septiembre han protagonizado movilizaciones callejeras exigiendo mejoras en el sistema educativo. Esta tarde, el jefe de Gobierno anunciará públicamente las medidas que ya ha comunicado a los jóvenes previamente.

Entre sus exigencias, los estudiantes reclaman una mayor inversión en los centros educativos, la contratación de profesores y una remodelación completa del sistema actual de acceso a la universidad, llamado Parcoursup , que según ellos "perpetúa las desigualdades" . En vistas de estas exigencias, el ministro de Educación Superior, Philippe Baptiste , ha anunciado que se llevará a cabo una "importante transformación" en 2027 del Parcoursup, y que el sistema será reemplazado en 2028.

No obstante, esta medida quedaría en manos de quien gobierne tras las próximas elecciones en primavera. Los estudiantes la han tachado de "insuficiente" y han confirmado que continuarán las protestas que perduran desde hace tres semanas. "Es un paso, pero hay que ir más lejos. "el Gobierno tiene miedo, ha demostrado que está desorientado", ha asegurado el portavoz de la asociación Les Lycéens, Louis Letoubon.

El presidente de la asociación estudiantil Renouveau Lycée, Nathanaël Combary, habla con la prensa  Firas Abdullah / EPA

El momento de mayor efervescencia de violencia en este mes de protestas se produjo el pasado 17 de octubre, cuando al menos 1.800 personas fueron arrestadas en unas movilizaciones que congregaron a unas 550.000 personas por todo el país. Lo que había comenzado como una revuelta estudiantil había pasado a convertirse en un movimiento nacional que involucraba también a sindicatos y a organizaciones como los " chalecos amarillos ".

El incidente más grave tuvo lugar en Limoges , donde un grupo incendió el histórico edificio del Ayuntamiento, del siglo XIX.

La semana pasada, el Gobierno anunció un despliegue "masivo" para controlar los disturbios que pudiesen producirse ese sábado, lo que suponía la entrada en escena de 70.000 agentes de policía. Estos refuerzos de los oficiales permitieron que no se repitieran los hechos violentos con la misma intensidad que en anteriores ocasiones, según el ministro de Interior,  Laurent Núñez . Sin embargo, Nuñez ha declarado que espera que se lleven a cabo más revueltas el próximo fin de semana.

El presidente francés, Emmanuel Macron , ha viajado a Marsella para inspeccionar los daños en las manifestaciones y transmitir solidaridad a los "afectados por las violencias del 17 de octubre": "Este sábado 24, el derecho a manifestarse ha sido preservado y el orden republicano ha sido mantenido. Nuestra determinación es total para que la calma perdure ", ha declarado en redes sociales.

El mandatario considera que "no es normal" que Francia "se encuentre en este estado de efervescencia" a seis meses de las elecciones presidenciales. Unos comicios en los que la extrema derecha, representada por Marine Le Pen, y la izquierda radical de Jean-Luc Mélenchon parten como las dos fuerzas más votadas, dejando fuera de escena a los partidos tradicionales. Ambos candidatos se muestran partidarios a reformar el sistema educativo actual por no favorecer el ascenso social. Es por ello que a los estudiantes no les preocupa demasiado que el Ejecutivo actual pretenda devolver la patata caliente al próximo mandatario.
sources.headline: El Gobierno franc�s anuncia medidas para poner fin a las protestas, pero los estudiantes las ven "insuficientes"

stories.headline: Former FBI director James Comey faces a third set of federal charges under Trump

sources.body:
Federal prosecutors have taken steps to charge ex-Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) Director James Comey with leaking national defence information, according to a court filing.

It marks the third time the justice department has moved to bring criminal charges against Comey, a longtime critic of President Donald Trump.

Few details are provided about the two counts in the three-page filing, but Comey's lawyers said in separate court papers that the case stemmed from an alleged disclosure of classified information to the New York Times in October 2016, while he was head of the FBI.

Comey denied any wrongdoing in a video posted on Substack on Monday, calling the charges an "appalling abuse".

"It would almost be funny if it weren't such an appalling abuse of the department of justice, one that we cannot become numb to," he said in the clip.

"Nothing's changed with me - I'm still innocent, I'm still not afraid of these people and I still believe in the independent federal judiciary."

Comey was charged in Washington DC through a criminal information, which is a formal written charging document filed directly by a prosecutor.

This is different to a criminal indictment, which must be approved by a grand jury, a group of citizens sworn in to review if evidence is strong enough to prosecute.

Comey's lawyer, Patrick Fitzgerald, said in a statement that two different teams of prosecutors had investigated the alleged disclosure to the New York Times a decade ago during the first Trump administration.

"Both times the Government determined that no charges should be brought against anyone," he said.

The attorney said the court filing "purports to charge Mr Comey with crimes that he did not commit".

His legal team has filed a motion to dismiss the charges.

Former federal prosecutor Glenn Kirschner told the BBC that the case may have exceeded the 10-year statute of limitations, giving the motion to dismiss the charges "a very good chance of being granted".

Kirschner said it seemed like the charges against Comey were a "revenge-fuelled attempt by Donald Trump to have his Department of Justice find something that might stick".

Comey was fired by Trump during his first term, after the former FBI director opened an investigation into claims of Russian meddling in the US 2016 presidential election.

Since then, Trump has repeatedly called for his prosecution, and these charges are the administration's third attempt to do so.

Comey was first indicted by a federal grand jury in September 2025 on charges that he had lied to Congress during testimony and obstructed a congressional proceeding.

He pleaded not guilty the following month before the case was dismissed in November.

In April 2026, Comey surrendered to authorities to face charges alleging that an image he briefly shared on social media posed a threat to Trump's life.

The case stemmed from a 2025 Instagram post by Comey, which contained a photo of seashells on a beach arranged to read "86 47".

"Eighty-six" is a slang term for "get rid of", and prosecutors allege it encourages violence against Trump, the 47th president.
sources.headline: Ex-FBI chief James Comey faces federal charges for third time

sources.body:
Comey, who was fired during Trump’s first term, has been accused of unlawfully divulging national security information.

James Comey, the former director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), is facing a third set of criminal charges under the administration of United States President Donald Trump.

On Monday, sealed documents came to light showing that the Trump administration has accused Comey of two counts related to the unlawful dissemination of “information related to national defence”.

Comey, a high-profile Trump critic, has not been indicted in the case. He has denied any wrongdoing.

But it is the third time the Trump administration has sought to level criminal charges against the former FBI director since the president returned to office in January 2025.

In an October court filing , prosecutors accuse Comey of ordering his FBI colleagues to leak information to the news media.

“The defendant [Comey] through one or more co-conspirators directed Individual #1 to disclose national defence information to a reporter for a national news publication,” the court filing reads.

In a video published on the online platform Substack, Comey once again denounced the Trump administration’s attempts to prosecute him as a campaign of political retribution.

“Well, now they’re back again. It would almost be funny if it weren’t such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice, one that we cannot become numb to,” Comey said.

“Nothing’s changed with me. I’m still innocent, and I’m still not afraid of these people, and I still believe in the independent federal judiciary.”

Comey also noted that Trump is only midway through his second term, and he hinted that he expects more criminal charges to come his way.

“The next couple years are going to be hard for all of us,” Comey added. “It’s really important that we stand straight and keep the faith in America.”

The latest charges pertain to a New York Times article from October 5, 2016, which describes how the email platform Yahoo was ordered to scan traffic on its site for a specific computer signature allegedly tied to a “terrorist” organisation.

Prosecutors have accused Comey of directing sensitive information to be disclosed to the reporter on that story, Charlie Savage.

In a statement released to news media, Comey’s defence lawyer Pat Fitzgerald framed the charges as feeble, claiming that the government had already investigated the matter twice before.

“Both times the Government determined that no charges should be brought against anyone,” the statement said.

Fitzgerald pointed out that government prosecutors had not sought an indictment, which involves presenting charges to a grand jury that must then choose whether to approve the criminal charges.

Instead, they are seeking to charge Comey through a process called a “criminal information”, which allows prosecutors to bypass a grand jury.

“Ten years after the article was published, the Government filed an ‘Information’ against Mr Comey that was not approved by a judge nor issued by a grand jury,” Fitzgerald said. “It purports to charge Mr Comey with crimes that he did not commit.”
sources.headline: Former FBI director James Comey hit with third set of charges under Trump

stories.headline: Trump offers a $1 million reward for tips leading to voter-fraud convictions before the midterms

sources.body: US President Donald Trump on Monday pledged a $1 million reward for information on voter fraud leading to conviction ahead of the upcoming 2026 US midterms on November 3. The president gave no details of how the reward would be funded or administered. The comments follow his repeated false claims that he won the 2020 presidential election.
sources.headline: Trump offers $1 million for tipoffs leading to vote fraud conviction as midterms approach

stories.headline: AI chatbots give less reliable election information to non-English-speaking voters, researchers warn

sources.body: AI chatbots are feeding non-native English speakers inaccurate information about the election, community activists and researchers warn, creating a barrier for some voters ahead of the midterms. The challenge — which leading AI companies say they’re working to address — is distinct from intentional disinformation campaigns that have plagued the internet for decades. Instead, some researchers and community leaders warn that voters prompting chatbots in non-English languages are unintentionally being fed inaccurate and ambiguous information — like whether they can vote by mail in their state — or overly literal translations that confuse electoral terms and lack context in various languages’ unique dialects. But the end result, the activists said, could still be the same: Voters whose native language is not English are more vulnerable to incorrect information and excluded from the most reliable answers ahead of the midterms. “Latino communities cannot afford to be left behind as artificial intelligence transforms how people work, learn, communicate and access information,” said Héctor Sánchez Barba, the president and CEO of Mi Familia Vota. “The history of the immigrant community and the Latino community has been one where we have been historically and structurally excluded from the best technology and access to information.” This digital divide has arisen, the activists and researchers say, in large part because AI models are trained in English, and fail to capture the nuances of other languages. Experts and grassroots organizations say this discrepancy in accuracy unintentionally disenfranchises non-English speaking voters across the country, where more than 20% of Americans speak a language other than English at home. National voter organizations that work in Latino and Asian American communities are grappling with how to bridge the gap and keep up with the rapidly developing technology to ensure that their communities don’t get left behind. Mi Familia Vota, which oversees some of the largest Latino voter mobilization efforts in the country, has built its own AI assistant dubbed “Nubi,” which comes from la nube or cloud in Spanish, for Spanish speakers seeking information on voting, voter registration and citizenship. The model is trained on government and nonpartisan datasets — as well as community data collected over 30 years of canvassing, town halls and citizenship workshops, said Denise Cook, chief innovation officer of Mi Familia Vota. She said it includes dialects of Mexican, Central American, South American and Caribbean Spanish, which have different words for election-related terminology. Polling place, for example, can be referred to as casilla , recinto or colegio electoral depending on the dialect, she said. Christine Choi, director of strategic communications at APIAVote, a civic engagement group for Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders, added that if AI fails to capture cultural and political nuances, “you can alienate a whole community or turn them off if you use the wrong interpretation.” A study by the Institute of Strategic Dialogue released in September found that accuracy of AI chatbots declined 16% when prompted in Spanish about voter information. Spanish prompts were more likely to produce incomplete or ambiguous answers, omitting relevant details and relying on overly literal translations, said Valeria de la Fuente Suárez, the lead author of the ISD study. “When voters are asking about registration deadlines or ID requirements, missing details can have real consequences,” she said. “Spanish-speaking voters deserve the same standards of clear, reliable and properly sourced information as English-speaking voters.” The study tested six frontier models through their respective APIs, or application programming interfaces, which are available for other developers to use. OpenAI, Anthropic and Google said in separate statements that they were working to refine their models for non-English languages, but APIs are not appropriate representations of how consumers interact with the actual chatbot interfaces, because they often include other fail-safes like popups or banners linking to external sources of information on voting. "Gemini is designed to respond with accurate and timely information and performed well in this analysis,” David Thompson, a spokesperson for Google, said in a statement. “However, this report accessed Gemini through our developer API, not the Gemini App, which has different protections and is how most people use our AI." Still, the leading AI companies say they are working to better provide election-related information to a wider swath of voters. To improve election information ahead of the midterms, OpenAI and Anthropic both said they are integrating information from Democracy Works , a nonprofit that collects official election information from the government, in its answers. “OpenAI's goal is to support people’s ability to participate freely in elections and make their own decisions with reliable information, transparency, and effective safeguards,” Nate Evans, a spokesperson for OpenAI, said in a statement. Some groups like Asian Texans for Justice, a nonprofit that works to increase voter engagement in Asian American communities in the battleground state, have opted to steer clear of the technology ahead of the midterms. “I do know that AI is being used more and more by AAPI communities, and we have made an organizational decision not to use AI for our in-language outreach due to inaccuracies,” said Nabila Mansoor, executive director of the organization. Spanish, Chinese and Vietnamese are among the most widely spoken languages in the U.S. besides English, but there are more than 500 other languages and language groups spoken across the country, according to the U.S. Census Bureau . The vast majority are considered low-resource languages with limited digitized data to train AI models, including Arabic, which has 1.3 million speakers in the U.S., and Swahili, which has about 150,000 speakers. And leading tech companies say they will try to address language-related access to AI systems more broadly. The Gates Foundation announced in September a coalition of 60 companies including OpenAI, Anthropic and Google dedicated to improving AI tools for an estimated 3.4 billion people around the world who speak languages underrepresented in AI models over the next five years. The joint commitment said, “The barrier is no longer the technology, which will only continue to improve. It requires a decision — to treat the world's languages as a shared foundation worth building, together, for everyone.” Community organizers say that while they welcome industry efforts to improve, the changes need to happen as soon as possible so immigrant communities can be equipped with the most reliable information for not only the midterms but the presidential election in 2028. “The way people get information has fundamentally changed and civic engagement has to change with it,” said Mi Familia Vota’s Barba.
sources.headline: AI has a language gap. That could be a problem for some voters.

stories.headline: Trump-spurned Republican incumbents withhold support from the party’s nominees

sources.body: Republicans spurned by President Donald Trump aren't interested in rescuing their would-be replacements. Instead, a growing number of retiring or ousted GOP incumbents from Nevada to North Carolina are sitting those races out, and in some cases, openly bucking their own party. Outgoing Sen. John Cornyn has raised money for various Republican Senate candidates — just not for Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who ousted him in the primary with support from Trump. He’s been vocal for months about what he sees as Paxton’s vulnerabilities and how Democrats could flip Texas blue for the first time in decades. North Carolina Sen. Thom Tillis — who has frequently criticized some of Trump’s Cabinet and broken with the White House on policy — has played little role in the campaign of former RNC Chair Michael Whatley, Trump’s hand-picked Senate candidate. The distance between the two Republicans is particularly notable as Whatley struggles to close the gap against Democrat Roy Cooper. Rep. Mark Amodei has repeatedly criticized, and now openly rejected voting for , the GOP nominee to replace him, David Flippo. “The bedwetting from outgoing moderate Republicans will define their legacy and only help socialists get elected,” said David McIntosh, president of the Trump-aligned Club for Growth, which has endorsed Flippo and Paxton. “People like John Cornyn and Mark Amodei need to get on board and support Republican nominees and stop posturing for an MSNOW contract.” But other Republicans defended their colleagues: “I never would question the loyalty to the party of Thom Tillis or John Cornyn. Both of them have contributed immensely to our party and our party's successes in the past and I suspect will be going forward,” said North Dakota GOP Sen. Kevin Cramer. “But I also don't begrudge them for their opinions and their right to be open about them.” These outgoing Republicans, several of whom were explicitly pushed out by Trump or persuaded to retire given his hold on the GOP, are using the midterms as a test: whether the party will demand loyalty to the president or can return to a pre-Trump era. “What [Trump’s] done is created a coalition that, in my opinion, will not stay with Republicans once we go back to traditional Republican platform priorities,” Tillis said in a recent interview with POLITICO . “A lot of the elements of the populism that Trump created to expand a base that made him successful running for president, I don't think that stays with the party long-term.” Some of those intraparty frustrations are starting to boil over, with Trump loyalist candidates and outgoing Republicans swiping at one another as Election Day barrels closer and the party’s overall fortunes look dire. The blame game is especially prominent in some of the Senate battlegrounds where Republicans have begun to quietly retreat in the final stretch of the midterms. Tillis never followed through on his offers to help Whatley by reaching out to holdout donors in the North Carolina Senate race, said one person familiar with the campaign who was granted anonymity to speak candidly about internal matters. "He was never part of our strategy because ... I mean, if he could have been helpful to us, then he could have ran," the person said, referring to Tillis' decision not to seek reelection last year. "The Tillis of the past year ain’t the same guy who worked overtime to help elect Republican majorities here in NC back in 2010." One person with knowledge of Tillis and North Carolina politics, also granted anonymity to speak candidly, countered that the outgoing GOP senator “doesn’t help sure winners or sure losers" and "Whatley has been a sure loser throughout 2026, running as Donald Trump’s ‘guy,’ and making zero effort to build his own brand." "All Whatley had to do was to keep this race competitive, but instead the party is facing a potential wipeout. This is an embarrassing effort by a former RNC chairman who only has himself and his consultants to blame for the completely avoidable beat down coming on Nov. 3," the person added. Spokespeople for Tillis did not respond to a request for comment. Whatley's campaign declined to comment. Natalie Baldassarre, a spokesperson for the Republican National Committee, touted the president’s endorsement record in a statement. More pointedly, she said that “Republicans who chose not to help elect other Republicans may as well be helping Democrats.” The White House did not respond to a request for comment. While the dynamic is less pronounced on the House side — Reps. Don Bacon and Elise Stefanik have been helpful to the Republicans running to replace them — there’s a clear exception: Amodei. Flippo, who’s trying to replace him, has dealt with a host of scandals, from stolen valor accusations to carpetbagging to campaign finance issues , but Trump’s endorsement helped boost him through the Republican primary in June . Top Republican outside groups, including Club for Growth, have poured millions into his race in Nevada’s 2nd District to rescue a seat the president won by 14 points in 2024. Amodei said in an interview that whoever was advising Trump to jump in and endorse Flippo gave “awful advice.” "The only criteria shouldn't be, ‘Well, they're the Republican,’” said Amodei, who cast his ballot for a third-party candidate this week. “I mean, politics is a team sport. But when a member of the team turns out to be this way, clearly this is not a bright and shining moment for the vetting process." Asked about Club for Growth president McIntosh's criticism of moderate "bedwetting," Amodei scoffed: "At least this crowd is absolutely consistent. Forget fundamental factual and character messes that campaigns won't and can't respond to; and attempt to change the focus to party loyalty," the retiring representative said. "Let me know when Club For Growth does a statement on campaign finance compliance, stolen Valor, and individual background transparency.” Even as figures like Cornyn and Amodei catch the fury of more Trump-aligned Republican forces for not falling behind the party line, that doesn't mean they’re abandoning fellow Republicans overall. Cornyn has raised more than $1.1 million at events in Dallas and Houston last month for the campaigns of Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Jon Husted of Ohio and Dan Sullivan of Alaska — as well as for the National Republican Senatorial Committee and other Senate candidates: Iowa Rep. Ashley Hinson, former Michigan Rep. Mike Rogers and former New Hampshire Sen. John Sununu, according to a person familiar with the senator’s political operation who was granted anonymity to discuss private events. He still clearly and explicitly draws a line against helping Paxton, telling reporters earlier this year, “Everything I said about him in the primary is true.” A spokesperson for Paxton did not respond to a request for comment. In Georgia, popular GOP Gov. Brian Kemp has been all-in on the governor’s race for Republican Rick Jackson — but he’s been comparatively quieter when it comes to Rep. Mike Collins’ Senate campaign to oust Democrat Jon Ossoff. The governor had initially recruited, backed and supported a different candidate in the GOP primary, though he’s since helped the Collins campaign with a public endorsement and by headlining a major fundraiser in Atlanta and others. Still, some Collins allies want the governor to be more involved. “Brian Kemp is someone who needs to be on the trail and someone who needs to help if Republicans are going to win,” said one GOP strategist working on races in Georgia who supports Collins and was granted anonymity to discuss internal dynamics. “But he did create some of this mess with the primary he ran against Mike who we all knew would be the nominee.” Meyer Sigfried, a Collins spokesperson, in a statement dismissed any suggestion that Kemp isn’t fully supporting Collins: “He’s been on the trail rallying Georgians to get out and vote early for Mike and Republicans up and down the ballot, and his help behind the scenes has been just as important.” A representative for Kemp referred POLITICO to Collins’ statement of support. Across the map, other frustrated Republicans have more directly pointed the finger at Trump for his interference, lambasting the president’s tendency to prop up candidates whom they deem too weak for the role. In South Carolina, Rep. Ralph Norman said this week he has refused to campaign with Sen. Darline Graham, who defeated him in the primary with Trump’s help. Graham has been under scrutiny for her lack of experience in elected office. Republicans still expect her to win in deep-red South Carolina, but they’ve also made late investments to shore up her campaign as Democrat Annie Andrews dominates in fundraising. Norman blamed the president , saying, "What he did to South Carolina … it's just not right,” but added he will still vote for Graham. T.W. Arrighi, a spokesperson for Graham, thanked the representative for his support in a statement, before hammering other Republicans — like Norman’s son, Warren Norman — who will not be voting for the GOP nominee: “It is unconscionable for anyone who claims to be a conservative in South Carolina to not vote straight ticket Republican and therefore endorse a Chuck Schumer-led Senate.” In many cases, GOP lawmakers are defending their disgruntled colleagues who have decided not to help Trump-picked candidates. "Folks have to follow their conscience. If a guy 'smells bad' then I wouldn’t,” said Bacon, who is supporting Brinker Harding, an Omaha city councilmember, in the race to replace him in his blue-leaning Nebraska district. "I like Brinker. He’s a good person."A “I believe we all ought to do all we can to help the good guys win the election,” Cramer added. “But I also understand people that ... feel aggrieved and want to maybe not be as enthusiastic about that as I am.” Mia McCarthy, Meredith Lee Hill and Aaron Pellish contributed to this report.
sources.headline: Spurned by Trump, these outgoing Republicans aren’t helping their potential successors

stories.headline: Spain relaxes environmental requirements for new data centers

sources.body:
La nueva propuesta de Real Decreto para regular los centros de datos en España mantiene los elementos clave del primer borrador, aunque da flexibilidad a las empresas en los tiempos para poner en marcha las medidas y otorga más plazo a las gigafactorías de IA europeas para vincularse a instalaciones renovables que provean al menos el 80 % del consumo de la infraestructura.

Fuentes del Ministerio para la Transición Ecológica y el Reto Demográfico (Miteco) recalcan que el nuevo texto mantiene "la ambición y los elementos clave" de la propuesta sometida a información pública para evitar los efectos adversos que un desarrollo descontrolado de las instalaciones produciría sobre los recursos hídricos y el precio de la electricidad.

El Gobierno ha enviado este lunes al Consejo de Estado el documento , que mantiene la exigencia a los titulares de los centros de datos de acreditar que cubran el 80 % de su consumo total mediante alguna de las modalidades de autoconsumo o a través de la compra de electricidad renovable ubicada en España.

Esta propuesta de decreto permite que las instalaciones renovables vinculadas puedan tener una antigüedad de hasta 36 meses previos a la puesta en marcha del centro de datos (frente a los 18 meses fijados en el primer borrador), así como también rebaja de 10 a 6 la duración de esos contratos.

Asimismo, la exigencia de cubrir al menos el 80 % del consumo total con energía renovable se flexibiliza al incorporar el almacenamiento con baterías y permitir que los centros de datos utilicen electricidad de plantas solares fotovoltaica s sin importar su fecha de construcción, siempre que estas no tuviesen suscrito uno o más contratos de compra de electricidad renovable a plazo a la entrada en vigor de este real decreto.

Hasta que empiece 2029, las empresas contarán con un plazo de gracia de seis meses desde la formalización del contrato de acceso a la red para cumplir estos requisitos de generación de energía eléctrica de origen renovable (adicionalidad, en términos técnicos).

Los centros de datos que "formen parte de iniciativas de la Unión Europea" y sean proyectos estratégicos europeos orientados a la soberanía digital tendrán de plazo hasta 60 meses para poner en marcha estas medidas de autoconsumo o compra de electricidad renovable, según destaca Efe.

Otro cambio respecto al primer borrador es el incremento del umbral general de aplicación de 1 a 10 megavatios (MW) de potencia de acceso, un cambio que centra el foco en los grandes centros de datos. Los centros con más de 10 MW de potencia eléctrica deberán consumir mayoritariamente energía renovable hasta que el mix energético en España sea un 90 % renovable, mediante autoconsumo o contratos de suministro a largo plazo.

Para cumplir los requisitos de correlación horaria renovable, las empresas podrán acogerse a un plazo de adaptación de cinco años con objetivos graduales a cambio de integrarse en el sistema de reducción automática de potencia para ser desconectados respetando el tiempo de respuesta comunicado por el operador del sistema sin indemnización ante tensiones en la red.
sources.headline: El Gobierno suaviza las exigencias ambientales para instalar centros de datos

sources.body:
Línea de servidores en un centro de datos de Microsoft

El Gobierno ha remitido este lunes al Consejo de Estado la última versión del real decreto para regular la instalación de los Centros de Procesamiento de Datos (CPD) en España, tras analizar las más de 600 alegaciones y el preceptivo informe de la CNMC al borrador que se elevó a consulta pública el pasado 25 de agosto.

El nuevo texto, al que ha tenido acceso La Vanguardia, mantiene los elementos clave expuestos en el borrador que buscan garantizar un despliegue ordenado para que la llegada de estas nuevas infraestructuras a España no tenga efectos negativos en la competencia por los recursos hídricos y que su presencia tenga los mínimos efectos posibles en la factura de los consumidores finales de electricidad, dado el elevado consumo de estas infraestructuras y su impacto en el sistema eléctrico. Pero hace modificaciones sustanciales respecto a la versión que se presentó a audiencia pública.

La primera de ellas es el perímetro al que afecta la norma, que ha pasado de ser todos los centros de datos cuya potencia de acceso sea igual a 1 MW a centrarlo solo en aquellos de 10 MW o más. Es decir, proyectos más grandes y con mayor capacidad financiera para cumplir con el requisito de consumir mayoritariamente energía renovable, ya sea mediante autoconsumo o con contratos de suministro a largo plazo (PPAs), hasta que España haya llegado a un determinado nivel de producción de renovables. En concreto, que el mix del país sea un 90% renovable.

Para ello, los proyectos que quieran optar a una conexión a la red eléctrica deberán justificar que llevan asociada nueva generación eléctrica para cubrir el 80% del consumo energético que vayan a realizar en cada una de las horas de funcionamiento. Eso sí rebaja la duración mínima de los PPA de 10 a 6 años y añaden expresamente las instalaciones de almacenamiento, es decir, baterías. Con lo que un centro de datos puede aprovechar las horas centrales del día con más producción solar para almacenar, en todo o en parte, la energía que utilizará durante la noche.

El requisito inicial hizo saltar las alarmas en el sector con la patronal Spain DC advirtiendo de la huida masiva de inversiones si no se modificaba y también fue cuestionado por la CNMC.

En atención a esas posiciones, el Gobierno lo mantiene para quienes sean capaces de llevarlo a cabo antes de la puesta en marcha del centro de datos, pero ha abierto un régimen transitorio de un plazo de cinco años, hasta 2031, para su cumplimiento. Los proyectos que se acojan a este régimen transitorio deberán cumplir unas condiciones. Por un lado, el porcentaje de generación asociada nueva y renovable que deben poner en marcha será del 60% del consumo, pero no en todas las horas, sino solo durante las horas punta de su nivel de tensión. Es decir, principalmente durante las noches, cuando la energía eléctrica es más cara y se dan los picos de demanda. Este requisito se extenderá hasta el 31 de diciembre de 2028. A partir de esa fecha y hasta el año 2031, el volumen de generación nueva y renovable que deben justificar será del 70% tanto en las horas punta como en las llano.
sources.headline: El Gobierno rebaja los requisitos para instalar nuevos centros de datos

sources.body:
Imagen del interior de un centro de datos / Agencias

El Gobierno revisa el real decreto que prepara para regular la actividad de los nuevos centros de datos y suaviza parcialmente las exigencias ambientales que pretende aplicarles, tras las c riticas de todo el sector tecnológico y energético y tras el informe crítico de la Comisión Nacional de los Mercados y la Competencia (CNMC) , en el que el regulador reclamaba moderar algunas de las obligaciones.

La nueva versión de la normativa, que el Ejecutivo ha remitido al Consejo de Estado para su estudio, mantiene la ambición de hacer una gran criba de la avalancha de proyectos de ‘data centers’ que hay en España (muy por encima de las previsiones de la propia industria y que resultan poco realistas) planteando nuevos requisitos verdes. El objetivo es que sigan adelante solo los más sostenibles y, a la vez, evitar que el gran consumo de luz de estas instalaciones y su impacto sobre el sistema provoque una gran subida de los precios eléctricos.

Pero la nueva versión del decreto del Gobierno también modera algunas de las exigencias más polémicas que se incluían en el primer borrador del decreto, da más tiempo para cumplir las obligaciones de consumo de electricidad renovable que habían levantado ampollas en el sector, y l imita su aplicación sólo a los centros de datos realmente grandes (sólo a los de más de 10 megavatios de potencia, mientras que en la primera versión era a todas las instalaciones de más de 1 megavatio), según confirman fuentes gubernamentales.

El objetivo del Gobierno sigue siendo poder aprobar el nuevo real decreto antes de las elecciones del próximo 29 de noviembre. Tras los comicios, el Gobierno en funciones no podría aprobar reales decretos salvo que se consideren de urgencia o que responden claramente al interés general. Si no llega a tiempo y no saca adelante el decreto antes del 29-N, la intención de Moncloa es pedir permiso a la Abogacía del Estado para poder hacerlo aún estando en funciones.

Los grandes centros de datos tendrán que garantizar que consumen mayoritariamente energía renovable mediante autoconsumo y contratos de suministro a largo plazo, hasta que el mix de producción español supere la cota del 90% de generación es renovable (algo que está previsto para dentro de una década). Entonces se entenderá que ya lo hacen de manera natural, simplemente consumiendo de la red. Pero el Gobierno ha abierto la mano y ha modulado las condiciones más estrictas que se planteaban hasta ahora.

La nueva versión del real decreto mantiene, en principio, la obligación de que los centros de datos garanticen que el 80% de la electricidad que consumen todas y cada una de las horas es de origen renovable (algo que las empresas tecnológicas consideran que son de imposible cumplimiento actualmente). Pero el Gobierno da a los centros de datos una prórroga de cinco años para cumplir esta obligación, a cambio de cumplir otros requisitos más laxos de manera transitoria.

Los nuevos ‘data centers’ podrán acogerse a un régimen transitorio de cinco años a cambio de participar en el sistema de reducción automática de potencia (SRAP), lo que permitiría a Red Eléctrica de España (REE) -el operador del sistema eléctrico- ordenarles que se desconecten de urgencia de la red y dejen de consumir luz en caso de ser necesario para evitar grandes desajustes. Los centros de datos que se acojan a esa posibilidad deberán cortar o reducir su consumo de la red (podrán seguir funcionando mediante baterías o sistemas de generación eléctrica propios), sin recibir ninguna compensación económica a cambio y asumiendo que serán las instalaciones que primero se desconectarán en caso de problemas.
sources.headline: El Gobierno suaviza el decreto de centros de datos y les da más tiempo para cumplir las exigencias verdes a cambio de poder desconectarlos

stories.headline: Spain begins returning Ceuta migrants to Morocco after denying their asylum claims

sources.body: <p>Los regresos no voluntarios de migrantes de Ceuta a Marruecos empiezan a ejecutarse. El Gobierno devolvió el viernes a 16 personas llegadas con la entrada masiva a la ciudad autónoma, la mayoría de origen subsahariano. Las administraciones ordenaron su retorno tras denegarles la solicitud de protección internacional, según confirman fuentes del Ministerio de Interior. Este es un escenario distinto al de los “retornos voluntarios” que se venían produciendo en suelo ceutí desde hace semanas. En su caso, a los citados 16 migrantes, “se les denegó la protección internacional” tras culminar la tramitación de sus expedientes. Tenían plazo para recurrir, “pero no lo hicieron”. Y, cumplido ese plazo, se les retornó al país vecino, según las mismas fuentes.</p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-26/el-gobierno-empieza-a-devolver-migrantes-de-ceuta-con-expedientes-judiciales.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>

stories.headline: Violent unrest spreads to Bilbao, with at least 19 arrests reported

sources.body:
La Ertzaintza ha detenido este lunes en Bilbao a 19 personas y ha investigado a otras tres por los altercados, con quemas de coches y contenedores y asaltos a algunos comercios , protagonizados por radicales que protestaban por un acto del creador de contenidos Vito Quiles , finalmente cancelado.

Entre los detenidos se encuentran siete menores de edad , tres jóvenes de 18 años y otro de 19, mientras que los ocho restantes aún se encuentran en proceso de investigación y las otras tres personas investigadas son un menor de 17 años y dos jóvenes de 22, según ha informado la Ertzaintza.

“ Imágenes de esta tarde en Bilbao. Un grupo de manifestantes ha incendiado varios contenedores, cinco coches y ha saqueado comercios. La Ertzaintza ha cargado y ha detenido a, al menos, 20 personas. https://t.co/MmfSWStKeh “

Los altercados, que han provocado numerosos daños en el mobiliario urbano y en locales de la ciudad, se han producido tras una concentración de varios miles de autodenominados 'antifascistas' que protestaban frente a la Universidad de Deusto por un acto convocado para las siete de la tarde en el que iba a intervenir Quiles, que anunció la cancelación del acto en sus redes sociales una media hora antes por razones de seguridad.

"Dado que hay exmiembros de ETA, terroristas callejeros y otros delincuentes encabezando las protestas, se suspende la charla. La libertad de expresión es sagrada, pero no más importante que proteger la integridad de todos los jóvenes de bien que acuden a estos actos y no merecen ser expuestos a situaciones violentas por culpa de una gentuza", ha argumentado Vito Quiles en su cuenta de X.

Tras disolverse sobre esa hora la concentración, varios cientos de radicales se han desplazado a la próxima avenida Lehendakeri Aguirre, donde han incendiado una motocicleta de la Policía municipal y decenas de contenedores de basura que habían desplazado al centro de la calzada, y después han lanzado piedras contra los agentes y la comisaría de la Ertzaintza en el barrio de Deusto.

Poco antes, un contenedor de obra había sido incendiado por los encapuchados en la calle Francesc Maciá, próxima a Lehendakari Aguirre, y habían lanzado cohetes y piedras contra los agentes de la Ertzaintza.

Posteriormente, los disturbios se han trasladado a la Plaza de Euskadi, junto al puente de Deusto, y al centro de la ciudad, donde los radicales han incendiado alrededor de media docena de vehículos y de nuevo numerosos contenedores.

El lehendakari Imanol Pradales ha expresado su "profunda preocupación" por estos altercados "intolerables" e "inaceptables" protagonizados por grupos de radicales, a los que ha dicho: "Ya basta. No los queremos en nuestro país ".

También el consejero vasco de Seguridad, Bingen Zupiria, se ha referido a estos hechos en declaraciones a ETB, donde ha opinado que "da la impresión de que alguien está queriendo emular movimientos violentos que vistos en otras partes de Europa", y ha lamentado que Euskadi esté asistiendo a "algo que creíamos olvidado" y que la sociedad vasca "no está dispuesta a aceptar".

Els magistrats han decretat l'internament en règim tancat per a tres dels menors detinguts aquest dissabte pels aldarulls al centre de Barcelona . Per a la resta dels que han passat per les instàncies judicials i ja s'ha resolt la seva situació, s'han ordenat diferents mesures cautelars compreses entre la llibertat vigilada i la prohibició d'assistir a manifestacions i reunions.

En relació amb els detinguts majors d'edat, 51 han passat aquest dilluns disposició judicial i tots ells han quedat en llibertat provisional amb mesures cautelars com comparèixer al jutjat o la prohibició d'assistir a manifestacions i reunions.

Estan acusats de desordres públics, danys, robatori amb força i atemptat contra agents de l'autoritat.

Els Mossos d'Esquadra van detenir per la seva vinculació amb els aldarulls de dissabte al vespre 130 persones, 76 de les quals són menors d'edat . La fiscalia havia demanat inicialment l'internament de sis dels menors detinguts, però de moment només es coneix que s'hagi decretat la mesura per a tres d'ells.

Encara no s'ha resolt la situació judicial de tots els menors detinguts, que s'anirà fent de manera progressiva segons el que estableix la llei del menor, com ha informat el Tribunal Superior de Justícia de Catalunya.

Aquest dilluns a la tarda s'ha detectat una nova convocatòria de mobilització a través de xarxes, al barri de Sants de Barcelona, però sense seguiment. El mateix va passar aquest diumenge a Granollers i Girona , on es van desplegar un dispositiu policial.

sources.body: (ACN) Tres dels menors detinguts pels aldarulls de dissabte a Barcelona han ingressat en centres de règim tancat. Es tracta dels casos més greus que la fiscalia ha posat a disposició dels jutges entre diumenge i dilluns . Dels que van passar diumenge, es va acordar règim tancat per a dos i mesures cautelars com ara la prohibició d’assistir a manifestacions i reunions i llibertat vigilada per a la resta. Dels que han passat dilluns s’ha acordat un internament en règim tancat i una llibertat vigilada. A banda, han passat a disposició judicial 51 majors d’edat . Per a tots s’ha decretat llibertat amb mesures cautelars que van des de la prohibició d’assistir a manifestacions i reunions a la via pública a Barcelona fins a compareixences al jutjat. stories.headline: Barcelona moves to identify and shut messaging groups used to promote the unrest

sources.body:
Els Mossos d'Esquadra demanaran autorització judicial urgent per investigar els administradors dels comptes de TikTok i de missatgeria a través dels quals es van convocar els joves que van provocar els aldarulls de dissabte al centre de Barcelona .

La consellera d'Interior, Núria Parlon , ha anunciat que posaran en marxa les "vies administratives i jurídiques" necessàries per exigir responsabilitats "als canals i a les plataformes responsables d'allotjar grups on s'incita a la violència, al pillatge i als desordres públics".

Parlon ha dit que demanaran "poder identificar les persones reals que hi ha darrere d'aquests missatges massius que s'han enviat" amb un objectiu molt clar:

Aconseguir que es tanquin aquests grups on s'està incitant els joves a la violència de forma clara, sense cap altre fi que cometre desordres públics i actuar amb violència.

De fet, el grup principal de Telegram , on hi havia uns 1.900 usuaris, ha estat clausurat aquest dilluns al vespre . La plataforma, que ha estat qui ha tancat el grup per incitació a la violència, diu que "no es pot mostrat el grup perquè ha violat les condicions d'ús".

Sobre la possibilitat que al darrere de les crides a provocar aldarulls hi hagi perfils vinculats a l'extrema dreta , Parlon ha subratllat: " Hem d'esperar i ser molt, molt curosos a l'hora de fer determinades apreciacions." I ha afegit que ara el que és "'important és deixar treballar la policia, que puguin fer les investigacions adequades".

Precisament aquest dilluns, s'havia convocat a través de xarxes una nova manifestació a plaça Espanya de Barcelona. La policia ha desplegat un dispositiu de seguretat a la zona, després de detectar que el cartell que circulava tenia la mateixa estètica que el de la convocatòria que va acabar dissabte amb greus aldarulls i 130 detinguts a la capital catalana.

Després de detectar-ho, els Mossos d'Esquadra i la Guàrdia Urbana han avisat als comerciants de la zona, que han protegit els aparadors o , fins i tot, alguns ha optat per abaixar la persiana . Tot i que no hi ha hagut aldarulls, els Mossos han identificat aquest dilluns a la tarda diversos joves a la zona.

La consellera d'Interior ha admès que dissabte la policia es va trobar amb una acció imprevista i que no anava precedida de cap manifestació.

Tot i això, ha assegurat que abans que comencessin els aldarulls i els saquejos a les botigues, els Mossos van identificar més de 300 joves "que portaven una determinada estètica i es van retirar materials que podien ser susceptibles de ser utilitzats en el marc d'aquesta concentració".

Núria Parlon ha afegit que, en aquests moments, la policia té molta informació que ara caldrà "endreçar per poder desarticular aquest grup que intencionadament està treballant amb aquesta finalitat de desestabilitzar i de crear una sensació d'inseguretat al conjunt de la població".

La consellera també s'ha referit a les crides que ja corren per xarxes per fer una nova concentració dissabte que ve a Barcelona. En aquest sentit, hi ha diversos perfils a Tiktok, creats diumenge, que escampen un nou cartell convocant una nova mobilització per dissabte que ve.
